source.title: What Causes Polysemanticity? An Alternative Origin Story of Mixed Selectivity from Incidental Causes
source.authors: Victor Lecomte; Kushal Thaman; Rylan Schaeffer; Naomi Bashkansky; Trevor Chow; Sanmi Koyejo

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether polysemanticity can arise from incidental training dynamics using toy autoencoders, rather than applying the original vision-neuron analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on superposition and polysemanticity, but the cited results are not rows. Results on sparsification alone (Figures 2, 4, and 5) are not recorded as polysemanticity outcomes: they measure sparsity proxies rather than mixed-neuron frequency.
record.test_reason: The paper argues and shows, in toy autoencoders, that polysemantic neurons arise from ℓ1 regularization or noise plus random initialization even when m ≥ n. That tests V4 directly and qualifies V3's capacity-pressure account.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also note that incidental polysemanticity can persist until the number of neurons is roughly the number of features squared, so adding neurons is not a practical fix. They suggest nudging training dynamics instead, for example by duplicating a neuron and adding noise.
record.recipe_differences: Uses shallow toy autoencoders with basis-vector data and studies incidental collisions caused by regularization or hidden-layer noise; it does not reproduce the original neuron-analysis method.
record.method_sensitivity: In the ℓ1 experiment, the reported number of polysemantic neurons varies with hidden-layer size m, following a Θ(n²/m) trend.

fits_no_version.finding: Bipolar noise (negative excess kurtosis) pushes encodings toward sparsity, while Gaussian noise has no observable sparsifying effect. Sparsity also grows with λ and σ, then drops at extreme values. These are fourth-norm sparsity proxies, not counts of polysemantic neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise-induced winner-take-all sparsity, a precondition for incidental polysemanticity, depends on the noise distribution's kurtosis.

record.problems: The evidence is from toy autoencoders rather than real-world networks. Polysemantic-neuron counts are shown in a figure rather than tabulated, and the specific noise example does not report an exact model size or a frequency across runs.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 2, 4, and 5 report sparsification or fourth-norm proxies, not polysemantic-neuron outcomes, so they are not included as rows.

untested.parts: Vision classifiers; no image models are studied.
Transformer language models, token or context responses, and layer differences.

Whether superposition causes polysemanticity when features outnumber neurons; the paper treats that account as non-exclusive and does not test it. How much real-network polysemanticity is necessary versus incidental is left open.
Real-world networks and how prevalent incidental polysemanticity is in them. Counts of polysemantic neurons under noise are not reported.
Activation functions, architectures, and the performance cost of reducing polysemanticity; the authors only propose this as future work.
Effects of activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label for V3 is too strong. The paper explicitly presents its account as non-mutually exclusive with superposition and never tests superposition cases, so limits_scope fits. The tranche is changed from T2 to T5 because the paper's core contribution is an argument that the standard origin story needs restating. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Transformer language models, token or context responses, and layer differences.
The paper tests an alternative source of polysemanticity in a toy autoencoder; it does not determine how much polysemanticity in trained networks generally is due to superposition.
Toy autoencoders only; no real-world networks or estimate of how prevalent incidental polysemanticity is in practice.
The share of polysemantic neurons across architectures or activation functions, and performance costs of reducing that share.
Whether canonical mixed-selectivity examples are better explained by shared features or related jobs.
How measurement range or explanation scoring changes polysemanticity judgments.

rows.subject: non-linear autoencoder
rows.size_stated: n ≈ 256 features; hidden-layer size m ranged from 256 to 4096
rows.operation_detail: Trained the autoencoder with ℓ1 regularization and counted polysemantic neurons across runs.
rows.value: The text reports a Θ(n²/m) trend; it says the constant 1/4 seems fairly accurate.
rows.note: The text says the trend held in experiments with n ≈ 256 and m from 256 to 4096. Since m ≥ n in this sweep, the reported polysemanticity does not require fewer neurons than features. Figure-level counts are not tabulated.
rows.check: Figure 3 caption gives n = 256 exactly. The value is the count of polysemantic neurons, which follows roughly n²/(4m) for m from 256 to 4096, all with m ≥ n. For V3 the row shows polysemanticity without any feature excess, so it bears on V3 only as a counter-case.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.5, Experiments paragraph: n ≈ 256, m from 256 to 4096, Θ(n²/m) trend holds, constant 1/4 fairly accurate. Figure 3 caption: 16 training runs, n = 256.

rows.subject: non-linear autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained the autoencoder with bipolar noise in the hidden layer.
rows.measure: Mixed feature encoding in neurons, described through shared coordinates of feature encodings
rows.value: The authors describe one encoding as having significant weights in 7 coordinates chosen by other encodings, with comparable absolute values; they attribute this configuration to interference interacting with the sparsity push.
rows.note: This is a specific illustrated instance, not a reported frequency. The text does not state the model's exact feature or hidden-layer size for this figure.
rows.check: This is a single illustrated instance with no frequency across runs. n and m are not stated for Figure 6, so it is unclear whether m ≥ n held. The record also does not mention that the mixed encoding (W2) spreads over 7 neurons already owned by other features, which is what makes those neurons mixed.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4 and Figure 6 caption (bipolar noise, σ = 0.01). W2 has significant weights in the 7 coordinates chosen by the other encodings.

relation.reason: Its own toy experiments and theory bear directly on V4, and on V3 by showing a second cause.

tranche.reason: The paper's central result and argument is that the superposition-only (capacity) account of polysemanticity is partial: there is a second, non-mutually exclusive origin. T5 fits.

source_check.notes: Noise results are qualitative: Figures 4-5 show sparsity only, and Figure 6 is one instance with no polysemantic-neuron counts. The authors say the Figure 6 mixing is 'significantly different' from the Section 2 collision type. Section 5 says incidental polysemanticity can persist until m is about n². The body gives n ≈ 256 and the Figure 3 caption gives n = 256.

statements.problem: Gives no number for this study by name.

Minor precision point: Figures 4-5 also give noise results (sparsification under bipolar vs normal noise at several σ). The Figure 6 instance is the only noise result on polysemanticity, which is what the statement means.
Same minor point: the only noise test of polysemanticity is Figure 6. Figures 4-5 test sparsity under noise at several σ.

Correct for this study (m 256 to 4096, n = 256, Θ(n²/m)). The phrase 'the one study that varies width' is a cross-study claim this text cannot check. The same statement cites 2211.09169 varying d, and V3.suggested_status credits 2211.09169 with a width sweep.
The open point about longer training is the synthesis's own framing, not from this paper, which does not state training length. That is acceptable as an open question.
